finding.claim: dropTable discards the result of Authorize(u, "dba"), so any authenticated user (any role) can reach the DROP TABLE path. This is an authorization bypass on a destructive admin endpoint.
finding.source: Any HTTP client that can reach POST/GET /admin/drop with a request context carrying a *User (any role). The attacker controls the request; the "dba" check is ignored.
finding.sink: runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27 (destructive DDL executed against the database)

trace.note: main registers /admin/drop -> dropTable with no auth middleware in this file
u := userFrom(r) - any user object present in the context is accepted
Authorize(u, "dba") return value is discarded; a "forbidden" error has no effect
r.FormValue("t") (query or body) concatenated into DDL and passed to runSQL
runSQL executes the string (stub here; real implementation not in the directory)

finding.guards_checked: (1) Authorize(u,"dba") at line 26: result unused, so the guard does not gate execution. Go accepts discarded error returns, so this compiles and vet does not block it by default. (2) userFrom at line 22: only confirms a user object exists, not a role. (3) No route-level middleware, role check, or method restriction in api.go. (4) No identifier allowlist or validation on "t" before concatenation. Compare vacuum at lines 33-36, which correctly returns on error; that is the pattern dropTable is missing.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare call whose error is discarded, so it does not gate dropTable. No route middleware, role check, or identifier allowlist exists in api.go:44-27. The vacuum handler at api.go:33-36 shows the correct pattern and is not applied here.
verdict.reason: Authorize's error return at api.go:26 is discarded, so dropTable (registered at api.go:44) runs runSQL("DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t")) at api.go:27 for any request whose context holds a *User, regardless of roles. Caveat: the middleware that populates the "user" context key is not in this directory, so the attacker must be an authenticated user of any role, which I could not verify, and runSQL is a stub at api.go:41.

finding.claim: SQL/DDL injection: the table name from r.FormValue("t") is concatenated into a DROP TABLE statement with no identifier validation or quoting. Even a legitimate dba user can inject additional SQL, such as stacked statements, if the driver allows multi-statement execution.
finding.source: r.FormValue("t") at api.go:27 - query string or form body, fully attacker-controlled.
finding.sink: runSQL at api.go:27 (string-built SQL executed by the database driver)

trace.note: r.FormValue("t") concatenated with "DROP TABLE " into one string
runSQL(string) receives the raw string; no parameterization path exists for identifiers

finding.guards_checked: No sanitization, allowlist of table names, identifier quoting, or prepared statement. The precondition is that the attacker reaches dropTable, which F1 makes possible for any authenticated user; with a fixed F1 this still requires the dba role. Severity is lower than F1 because it needs dba, or F1 unfixed.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. Authorize (api.go:13-20) is called at api.go:26 as a bare statement and its error is discarded, so dropTable runs for any authenticated user (this is F1). No identifier allowlist, quoting, or parameterization exists between r.FormValue("t") (api.go:27) and runSQL (api.go:41), which is an empty stub taking a raw string.
verdict.reason: The "t" form value is concatenated into "DROP TABLE " at api.go:27 and passed unvalidated to runSQL at api.go:41, and because the Authorize result is discarded at api.go:26, any authenticated user reaches this sink. The stacked-statement sub-claim cannot be verified because runSQL is a no-op stub, and the "legitimate dba user" framing adds little, but the injection itself is real.

finding.claim: Authentication is assumed, not enforced. userFrom performs an unchecked type assertion on the request context value "user". Nothing in this file sets that value or registers authentication middleware, so every request to /admin/* panics. This is a robustness and availability defect, and a deployment-dependency risk if the middleware is missing or misconfigured.
finding.source: Any HTTP request to /admin/drop or /admin/vacuum; the context key "user" is set outside this file, if at all.
finding.sink: Unchecked assertion .(*User) at api.go:22 (panic on nil or wrong type); the protected operations are dropTable and vacuum.

trace.note: routes registered with no auth wrapper
r.Context().Value("user").(*User) - panics if the value is absent or not *User

finding.guards_checked: No middleware or ok-form assertion in this file. The string context key "user" is also a collision risk (staticcheck SA1029 flags it). net/http recovers per-request panics, so the impact is limited to request-level failures unless the assertion is relied on as the only auth gate, in which case the protection is absent altogether.

verdict.guard_found: none. No middleware or context.WithValue("user") exists in the directory (Grep finds only api.go:22, 25, 32). Routes at api.go:44-45 have no wrapper. The only other control is net/http's per-request panic recovery, which contains the panic to that request but does not prevent it.
verdict.reason: Anonymous requests to /admin/drop (api.go:44, via dropTable at api.go:25) and /admin/vacuum (api.go:45, via vacuum at api.go:32) reach the unchecked assertion at api.go:22 with no value set under "user", so they panic before any effect; the claim is accurate as stated but is a request-level robustness defect, not a bypass. The candidate misses a more serious issue in the same file: dropTable at api.go:26 discards Authorize's error, and api.go:27 concatenates r.FormValue("t") into SQL. If a middleware sets "user" outside this directory, any authenticated user could reach the DROP TABLE path.

finding.claim: The admin server is bound to all interfaces (":8083") over plaintext HTTP with no TLS and no authentication middleware visible in the file, and the ListenAndServe error is ignored. Exposure depends on deployment and network controls outside this directory.
finding.source: Network clients that can reach port 8083 on any host interface.
finding.sink: http.ListenAndServe(":8083", nil) at api.go:46 exposing /admin/drop and /admin/vacuum.

trace.note: ListenAndServe binds to all interfaces with the default mux and no TLS

finding.guards_checked: No TLS, no bind address restriction, no auth wrapper, no error check on ListenAndServe. Confidence is lower than F1-F2 because the surrounding network or proxy configuration is not in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: api.go:33-35: vacuum checks Authorize(u, "dba") and returns 403 on error, so /admin/vacuum requires the dba role. api.go:22: userFrom type-asserts a *User from request context, so there is no anonymous path in this file. The /admin/drop path has no effective guard, but that is because api.go:26 discards Authorize's result, which is the F1 issue, not the bind address.
verdict.reason: The trace lines at api.go:44-46 are accurate, but the claimed exposure is not independent of the bind address: /admin/vacuum is gated by an effective, checked role check at api.go:33-35, and the only unguarded effect (/admin/drop at api.go:26-27) is caused by the discarded Authorize result, not by ":8083" on all interfaces. The network-exposure claim also depends on deployment config outside this directory.
